title: Sharded Attention Execution Guidelines
author: Asha Nayar
body:
Summary:
This guide describes recommended execution patterns, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling steps, benchmark integration notes, and operational runbook actions for sharded-attention execution in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for engineers who implement or tune shard-aware kernels, SREs triaging performance regressions, and platform owners running the benchmarking suite.

Goals:
- Provide a compact, actionable checklist to achieve predictable latency and throughput for sharded attention workloads.
- Describe scheduling primitives and policy knobs the runtime exposes and when to use them.
- Outline profiling and benchmark procedures that produce reproducible performance artifacts.
- Document triage/runbook steps for common regressions and known mitigations.

Context and background:
Sharded attention (tensor-parallel splits across KV shards) is used for large-decoder models and some encoder-decoder variants to scale state and computation. In our fleet, sharded attention adds interaction points with: GPU memory placement, KV cache routing, communication schedules (all-reduce / reduce-scatter), and kernel selection (FP16 vs int8 mixed paths). Mistuned scheduling or batching can produce amplified tail latency and cross-request interference.

Architecture overview (high level):
- Logical components:
  - Request router: assigns incoming requests to shard groups based on model-version and shard topology.
  - Execution orchestrator: slices requests into micro-batches for compute kernels and coordinates cross-shard comms.
  - Kernel mapper: selects kernel variant based on seq_len distribution, quantization profile, and available comm topology.
  - KV cache manager: handles prefix cache hits, partial cache reuse and eviction across shards.

- Dataflow sketch:
  1) Request arrives -> route to shard-group leader
  2) Orchestrator computes micro-batch plan (batch size, slice offsets)
  3) KV indices resolved; cross-shard comm plan computed
  4) Kernels invoked on each shard with coordinated comm primitives

Key scheduling primitives and policies:
- Priority lanes: per-tenant/per-route numeric priority (0..7). Use lanes to isolate high-SLO customers from best-effort workloads.
- Deadline-aware slicing: requests with tight latency budgets can be sliced into smaller micro-batches that avoid queueing behind large batches. Config knob: scheduler.deadline_slicing.enabled (boolean) and scheduler.deadline_slicing.max_slices (int).
- Backpressure thresholds: two soft thresholds (queue_soft_ms, queue_hard_ms). If queue latency exceeds queue_soft_ms the scheduler reduces auto-batched slice sizes by 25% until below threshold. If queue_hard_ms is exceeded the request is re-routed to fallback model variant.
- Affinity constraints: pin hot shard leaders to NIC/GPU pairs to reduce cross-host comm overhead for latency-sensitive flows. affinity.policy can be set to host-local | spread | packed.

Kernel selection heuristics (how mapper picks kernels):
- Inputs considered: seq_len distribution (p50/p95/p99), effective micro-batch size, quantization profile, active comm topology.
- Heuristic examples:
  - If p95_seq_len < 64 and micro-batch >= 8 -> choose fused-attention-kernel-v2 for stable throughput.
  - If quant_profile == int8 and there are frequent prefix-cache-hits -> prefer int8-kernel-with-cache-optimized-path to reduce decode overhead.
  - If all-reduce latency > 120us -> choose locality-optimized kernels that favor reduce-scatter + overlap-compute.

Profiling and investigation playbook (step-by-step):
1) Reproduce on staging with the same model-version and shard-topology. Record the exact git commit / runtime image.
2) Capture end-to-end traces for 5k requests across representative traffic: use agent tracing (trace level = debug) and kernel-level telemetry. Commands:
   - rwinfctl trace start --model my-model:2026-02-01 --duration 10m --level debug --out /tmp/trace-$(date +%s).zip
   - nvprof (for local reproduce) or perf on host; capture GPU kernel timelines.
3) Produce flamegraphs for the orchestrator and per-GPU kernel timelines. Tools and scripts: scripts/perf/trace_to_flame.sh /tmp/trace.zip > /tmp/flame.svg
4) Validate comm microbench: run inter-shard all-reduce ping-pairs to measure baseline latency (expected < 80us in colocated racks).
5) Compare metric deltas vs baseline: p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, GPU occupancy, SM utilization, PCIe bandwidth.
6) Run focused microbench with synthetic seq_len slices to isolate kernel selection boundaries. Use the benchmarking harness: 
   - benchctl run --workload sharded-attn-sweep --model my-model --seq-lens 8,32,128 --micro-batch-sizes 1,4,8 --out ./bench-results.json
7) If kernel hotpath spans >20% of observed latency and comms are under budget, open a kernel ticket and include reproducible microbench steps (see "Ownership and escalation").

Benchmarking suite notes (integration and expectations):
- Canonical workloads: sharded-attn-sweep (sweeps seq lens and micro-batches), long-prefix (emulates long prefix reuse), mixed-traffic (production mix weighted by route).
- Metrics to publish per run (JSON fields required): run_id, model_version, shard_topology, seq_len_p50/p95/p99, tokens_per_sec_mean, tail_latency_ms_p99, gpu_utilization_mean, comm_latency_us_mean.
- Acceptance criteria for a candidate kernel change: tokens_per_sec >= baseline * 1.02 OR tail_latency_p99 <= baseline * 0.98, with no increase in memory-footprint > 5%.
- Artifact retention: keep raw traces and kernel timelines for at least 90 days for any benchmark that triggers a perf regression alert.

Operational runbook snippets (common incidents):
Incident: sudden p99 spike for sharded models across a rack
  1) Check scheduler queue depth and queue_soft_ms/queue_hard_ms events in the last 30 minutes.
  2) Validate inter-shard all-reduce latency from telemetry. If > 150us, escalate to networking and check NIC interrupts/traffic shaping.
  3) If comms healthy, inspect kernel selection logs for unexpected switch to slow kernel variant (kernel_mapper.log).
  4) Hot mitigation: enable priority lane for affected routes (rwctl route update <route> --priority 1) and reduce batch windows for that node group (set scheduler.batch_window_ms = 3).
  5) If mitigation fails, failover affected routes to fallback model variant with local (non-sharded) execution: route->fallback:model:local-encoder-compat.

Incident: long running fragmentation / OOMs on shard GPUs
  1) Run host-diagnostics to capture GPU memory fragmentation metrics.
  2) If fragmentation ratio > 0.65, schedule a rolling drain of the host, trigger unified-allocator defrag (adminctl allocator defrag --target gpu0).
  3) If OOM persists, reduce per-shard KV cache retention for that model (kvcache.retention_ms = 600000).

Known issues and current mitigations (as of runtime v3.4.x):
- Issue: intermittent 10–20% p99 degradation when sequence-length distribution shifts suddenly toward long prefixes.
  - Mitigation: enable adaptive_kernel_mapper.seq_len_smoothing to avoid thrashing kernel selection.
- Issue: all-reduce tail latency anomalies correlated with kernel preemption on mixed workloads.
  - Mitigation: set affinity.policy=packed for latency-critical routes and move large-batch offline traffic to dedicated nodes.
- Issue: int8 cache-path regressions when cache eviction patterns align with quantized tile boundaries.
  - Mitigation: use fallback quantization profile int8-stable for models with >10% prefix reuse until kernel patch is released.

Release notes snapshot (runtime v3.4.2):
- Improved locality-optimized kernels for 8x shard topologies; expected comm latency reduction ~18% for colocated racks.
- Added deadline_slicing scheduler knob and two new telemetry counters: scheduler.slice_count and scheduler.slice_drop_rate.
- Fixed memory leak in fused-attention-kernel-v1 when micro-batch size == 1.

Ownership and escalation:
- Kernel mapper and scheduling primitives: Runtime Core team (team lead: Miguel Santos).
- Benchmarks and profiling harness: Bench Team (owner: Sofia Ramos).
- SRE operational playbooks: Platform Reliability (lead: Liam O'Connor).
- Escalation path: On-call runtime engineer -> Runtime Core -> Networking -> Kernel dev. Use the incident-runbook channel for urgent comms.

Adding a new kernel variant (developer checklist):
1) Implement kernel and add feature flag kernel.<name>.enabled=false by default.
2) Add unit-level microbench in bench/harness (sharded-attn-sweep).
3) Run full benchmark matrix on staging and publish artifacts to /bench-artifacts/<run_id>.
4) Open a PR with documentation entry in this guide and a migration note for operators.
5) Iterate on heuristics and land default enablement only after 2 successful benchmark runs with artifacts reviewed by Bench Team.

References and links:
- Kernel mapper design doc: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/adaptive-kernel-mapper-and-scaling-playbook-2026
- Shard topology reference: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-op-pathways-and-shard-topology-2024
- Benchmarking harness README: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/throughput-latency-workload-catalog-2026

Appendix: Quick config table (YAML-like example)
| key | example value | description |
| scheduler.deadline_slicing.enabled | true | enable slicing for tight-latency routes |
| scheduler.deadline_slicing.max_slices | 6 | max micro-slices per request |
| scheduler.batch_window_ms | 6 | how long to wait for auto-batching (ms) |
| affinity.policy | host-local | affinity placement policy (host-local|spread|packed) |
| kvcache.retention_ms | 600000 | default per-model KV cache retention |

If you make changes to this doc, update the related_pages list and add the bench run_id that validates the change.
summary: Guidelines and operational playbook for sharded attention execution, kernel mapping, profiling flows, benchmarking integration, and triage steps for performance incidents.
